storm.summary_layperson: No storms are currently tracking toward the cove, but instability is building through the evening, keeping a slight chance of a thunderstorm in play through the window.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The marine layer holds an 8°F air–water gap at 5 PM but weakens to about 3°F by 8 PM as the air cools — the buffer is essentially gone right around when instability is forecast to peak this evening.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar shows a cluster of cells (up to 64 dBZ) 35–48 miles to the west and southwest, but nearly all of them are tracking away from the cove — measured storm motion is toward the NW at about 12.5 kt — with one cell 39 miles WSW essentially stationary relative to Greenwich. Nothing is currently closing on the cove. CAPE is modest right now (300 J/kg) but the HRRR forecast has it building to roughly 1,560 J/kg by 8 PM alongside 29–35 kt of deep-layer shear, which is enough on its own to elevate the risk call for the back half of the window even with radar quiet at the moment. That lines up with this afternoon's NWS Upton (OKX) forecast discussion, which flags "two rounds of showers and thunderstorms with marginal severe potential" and scattered storms possible "from the NYC metro on west" later this evening. The official forecast carries a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms after 5 PM.

The Sound's cool water (74°F vs 82°F air, an 8°F gap right now) normally sets up a stabilizing marine layer that can weaken storms crossing it before they reach shore. That gap is fading fast tonight: it drops below the ~5°F protective threshold around 7 PM and keeps sliding negative overnight as the air cools faster than the water. Since the CAPE buildup that matters most doesn't peak until roughly 8 PM, any storm that actually develops and heads this way later tonight would be arriving into a cove with little or no marine-layer buffer left.

Net effect: with no cell currently tracked toward Greenwich, near-term risk is low, but as new cells may fire later this evening with rising instability and strong shear, the moderate call reflects that building potential rather than an active threat right now. Because no Sound-crossing storm is in play at the moment, the cove isn't clearly better or worse off than inland towns tonight — that would change if a new cell forms and tracks in from the west while some marine-layer buffer still exists (before ~7 PM).

What would change the call: a new cell developing to the west or southwest and tracking ENE/NE toward the cove, especially before 7 PM while the marine layer still has some bite; a severe thunderstorm or tornado warning posted for southern Fairfield/Westchester counties; or an upstream APRS gust spike at the Rye/Port Chester stations signaling an approaching outflow boundary.

wind.tactics_blurb: RYC now: S 189° at 4 kt (10-min avg 4, gusting 7). Light gradient wind with no sea breeze organized today — expect a drifter evening in the 2–5 kt range wandering between S and WSW rather than a clean thermal build. Stay centered on the course and play each shift; no side is reliably favored in wind this light and unsettled.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The air–water temperature difference (deltaT) is 8.3°F, comfortably clearing the 5°F sea-breeze threshold, but the pipeline's own thermal proxy says the sea breeze isn't actually organized today — only 35% of coastal stations are showing a southerly signal, below the bar for calling it "active," so this lands as a gradient-only day (Regime B) rather than a thermal one, regardless of the promising deltaT. The gradient itself is light: the authoritative station average is 7.5 kt, just under the cutoff for a solidly raceable gradient day, putting tonight in the light-gradient bucket.

RYC currently reads S 189° at 4.3 kt (10-min avg 4.1), gusting 7 — soft. The cove's own cluster of stations (the western-LIS group) actually shows a fairly consistent SW 228° with strong internal agreement, but that consensus is diluted once the broader coastal ensemble (including Long Island's north shore, which isn't seeing the same southerly push) is folded in — agreement there drops to 0.71. HRRR's raw hourly direction is itself unsettled, swinging from SSW to WSW to S to SSW to WSW to SW across the window, which reads more as weak, directionally uncommitted flow than a developing sea breeze. Worth flagging: HRRR's current-hour direction (SSW 198°) is running about 30° behind what stations are actually showing (SW 228°) — a divergence large enough to matter, though since this isn't a sea-breeze day the usual maturation correction doesn't apply; treat the observed direction as the better read for right now.

Because there's no thermal engine running, the usual sunset-collapse story doesn't apply — this isn't wind that's going to die at 7:28 PM, it's wind that's already light and wandering now and likely stays that way. Sunset is at 7:58 PM; expect the flow to stay in the 2–5 kt range through and past it, with a chance it goes fully variable for stretches as the boundary layer stabilizes after dark.

Racing translation: 2–5 kt with gusts to 7–8 kt is drifter territory for most one-design fleets all evening — finicky, patient sailing rather than powered-up racing. With direction bouncing between S and WSW and no station showing a clear, sustained advantage on either shore, there's no side to bank on; staying centered and reacting to each header/lift will beat committing early to one edge of the course.
